name: borrowed days

attributes.attribute: also called the Skinning Days in the west of Ireland
cow of abundance also called the Old Brindled Cow or Gray Cow
defied winter and was skinned in retaliation

sources: Danaher, Kevin. *The Year in Ireland*. Cork: Mercier Press, 1922, 85.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Borrowed days form a mythic theme. These are the stormy days of late spring. Winter seems to come back to life then. People once called them the Borrowed Days. They were also named the Skinning Days. This usage was current in the west of Ireland. Legend tells of the Glas Ghaibhleann. That cow of abundance had other names. Some called it the Old Brindled Cow. Others called it the Gray Cow. It defied winter by claiming winter could not kill it. Winter then stole several days from spring. It skinned the cow in retaliation.

okr.objective: Describe borrowed days and the legend of the cow that defied winter.
key_results: Borrowed days are the stormy days of late spring.
The name was also the Skinning Days in the west of Ireland.
The Glas Ghaibhleann was the cow of abundance.
Winter stole days from spring and skinned the cow in reply.
okr.evidence: Monaghan 2008, s.v. 'borrowed days'; Danaher 1972, 'The Year in Ireland'.
